units.title: Basic Concept of Sociology
topics: Relationship of sociology with other social sciences
Why sociology matters to computer professionals

sections.title: Relationship of sociology with other social sciences
Why sociology matters to computer professionals

summary: Sociology, named by Comte in 1838, is the scientific study of society, social relationships, institutions and social behaviour.

Durkheim (social facts), Weber (social action and meaning), MacIver and Page (social relationships) give the classic definitions; Mills' sociological imagination links personal troubles with public issues.
Its nature: a social, empirical, theoretical, cumulative, general and (in aim) value-neutral science, both pure and applied.
Functionalism (order and function), conflict theory (power and inequality) and symbolic interactionism (meaning and interaction) are the three main perspectives.
The formal school limits sociology to forms of relationships; the synthetic school makes it a general science of society.
Sociology is closest to anthropology and social psychology, and connects to economics, politics, history, geography and computing.

units.title: Organizing Social Life
topics: Technology and the organisation of social life

sections.title: Technology and the organisation of social life

summary: A society is a web of social relationships; a community adds locality and community sentiment. Nepal (Census 2021) has 29,164,578 people, 4.37 per household and an uneven distribution across provinces.
Culture is learned, shared, cumulative, symbolic and adaptive; material and non-material parts change at different speeds (cultural lag). Avoid ethnocentrism; use relativism to understand.
Values give direction; norms (folkways, mores, taboos, laws) enforce them through sanctions and social control.
Status is a position (ascribed, achieved, master), role the expected behaviour; role conflict is between roles, role strain within one.
Marriage, family and kinship are the core institutions of social life; the Nepali family is shifting from joint to nuclear and transnational forms.
Groups: primary and secondary, in-group and out-group, reference and formal and informal groups; Nepal has guthi, parma, dhukuti and aama samuha.

units.title: Social System and Social Stratification of Nepalese Societies
topics: Social and cultural change in Nepal

sections.title: Social and cultural change in Nepal

summary: A social system is an organised pattern of statuses, roles, groups and institutions. The social processes are cooperation, competition, conflict, accommodation and assimilation; socialisation turns a newborn into a member of society (Cooley, Mead, Freud, Piaget).

Social change alters structure and relationships; cultural change alters beliefs, language and technology. In Nepal the main factors are politics, law, education, migration, technology and media, infrastructure, disasters and rights movements.

Stratification is a ranking of people into layers with unequal rewards. Nepal's formal caste hierarchy (Muluki Ain 1854) was abolished by the Muluki Ain 1963; discrimination persists and is criminalised.
Caste, ethnicity, gender, religion and ecology each create unequal access, and they overlap.
National integration moved from imposed assimilation (one language, one dress, one nation) to unity in diversity under the 2015 constitution.

summary: Society, culture and structure change under many forces, technology among them; technology comprises artefacts, knowledge and organisation.
Determinism, SCOT, co-production and ANT give four lenses; Winner's point is that designs carry politics.
Information revolutions run from writing and printing to mobile, data and AI; Nepal leapfrogged fixed lines.
Moore's law (doubling every ~2 years, √2 − 1 = 41.4% per year) explains the rapid fall in cost of computing; it is a trend, with physical limits.
Social impacts are mixed in every domain; ask who benefits, who pays and who is absent.

units.title: Technology Adoption and Diffusion of Innovations
topics: Seeing the ideas: adoption in hardware, TAM, adopter categories and the two growth curves

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: adoption in hardware, TAM, adopter categories and the two growth curves

summary: TAM: PU and PEOU drive intention; UTAUT adds social influence and facilitating conditions; trust matters in Nepal.
Cronbach's alpha checks scale reliability; correlated predictors (multicollinearity) limit what a small regression can tell.
Rogers' categories come from the normal curve (2.5, 13.5, 34, 34, 16%); the five attributes of innovations predict speed.
The logistic curve peaks in rate at t₀; the Bass model combines innovation (p) and imitation (q) with peak time ln(q/p)/(p+q).
Barriers are individual, organisational, technical, social and policy-related; respect and participation lower resistance.

units.title: The Digital Divide and Digital Nepal
topics: Seeing the ideas: the infrastructure, the three levels, the Lorenz curve and the index

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: the infrastructure, the three levels, the Lorenz curve and the index

summary: The divide has three levels (access, skills, outcomes) and many dimensions: geography, income, gender, age, disability, language and caste.
Gaps, ratios, the gender parity index, Lorenz/Gini and min-max composite indices measure it; the unit of analysis and the method must be stated.
Unicode, Nepali-language tools and local content are conditions for benefit, not extras.
The Digital Nepal Framework (2019) has eight sectors: Digital Foundation, Agriculture, Health, Education, Energy, Tourism, Finance and Urban Infrastructure.
Closing the divide needs infrastructure, affordability, skills, local content, inclusive design and trust, and assisted channels.

units.title: Cyberethics, Privacy and Algorithmic Fairness
topics: Algorithmic bias: where it comes from
Seeing the ideas: faces, pipelines, rates and trade-offs

sections.title: Algorithmic bias: where it comes from
Seeing the ideas: faces, pipelines, rates and trade-offs

summary: Utilitarian, duty, virtue and care frameworks, plus the ACM and IEEE codes, structure ethical decisions; refuse, document and escalate when asked to do wrong.
Everyday cyberethics covers privacy, misinformation, harassment, plagiarism, piracy and netiquette.
Bias enters through history, sampling, measurement, labels, aggregation and deployment; proxies defeat attribute removal.
Fairness metrics (demographic parity, disparate impact, equal opportunity, equalized odds, predictive parity) are computed from group confusion matrices and can conflict when base rates differ.
Responsible systems are transparent, explainable, contestable, accountable and audited.

Social and cultural bases of technological change
Process and patterns of diffusion of innovation
Consequences of technological development on Nepalese society
Accountability of computer professionals towards society

summary: A technological society is one in which technology and technical knowledge drive the economy, organisation and everyday life (Bell: post-industrial; Toffler: third wave; Ellul: technique; Castells: network society). Nepal is a society in transition with old and new features side by side.

In Third World societies, technology is mostly imported, so transfer, dependency, appropriate technology and leapfrogging are the key ideas. Technology works only if it fits local conditions and institutions.

The social and cultural bases of technological change are economic, political, educational, social-structural, cultural, linguistic, community and geographic. Cultural lag appears where tools outrun norms and laws.
Innovations diffuse through knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation and confirmation; opinion leaders and the five Rogers attributes decide the speed.
Consequences on Nepal are mixed: remittance and digital economy, connection and education on one side; inequality, misinformation, e-waste and crime on the other.
Computing professionals are accountable for safety, privacy, honesty, fairness, intellectual property, environment and public good; codes of ethics and national laws guide them.
Social research moves from problem and hypothesis through design, data collection and analysis to report, with ethics throughout.

units.title: Cyber and IT Law in Nepal
topics: Seeing the ideas: the institutions, the penalty ceilings, the trust chain and the first hour

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: the institutions, the penalty ceilings, the trust chain and the first hour

summary: Cyber law supplies recognition (records, signatures), crime definitions and rights; jurisdiction and evidence are enduring difficulties.
The ETA 2063 recognises electronic records and digital signatures, creates the Controller of Certification and Certifying Authorities, and defines computer offences.
Sections 44, 45 and 46 carry up to 3 years and Rs 2,00,000; section 47 up to 5 years and Rs 1,00,000; section 52 (computer fraud) up to 2 years and Rs 1,00,000.
The Individual Privacy Act 2075, the Copyright Act 2059, the Criminal Code 2074 and the 2080 cyber security policy complete the framework.
Professionals act within authorisation, protect data, respect licences and preserve evidence.

units.title: e-Governance in Nepal
topics: Seeing the ideas: the front desks, the four models, the index, the savings and the signature

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: the front desks, the four models, the index, the savings and the signature

summary: e-Governance covers service delivery, transparency and participation; models are G2C, G2B, G2G and G2E; maturity runs from emerging to connected.
EGDI-style indices average service, infrastructure and human-capital components; cost-benefit estimates should count citizens' time and access.
Nepali building blocks: National ID, Nagarik App, GIDC and office systems, tax, customs and procurement portals, and Palika software.
A digital signature hashes the document and transforms the digest with the private key; a CA's certificate binds the public key to the identity.
Success depends on inclusion, security, interoperability, legal safeguards and reengineered processes.

topics: The life cycle of a device
Seeing the ideas: the fires, the sorting line, the aisle, the flows and the footprint

sections.title: The life cycle of a device
Seeing the ideas: the fires, the sorting line, the aisle, the flows and the footprint

summary: E-waste contains hazardous and valuable materials; informal burning harms health; most Nepali e-waste is stored or processed informally.
A device's footprint is front-loaded (manufacture), so longer life, repair and reuse beat recycling, which beats disposal.
Manage e-waste by reduce, reuse, recycle, EPR and the Basel framework; sanitise data before disposal.
PUE = total ÷ IT power (DCiE is its reciprocal); energy = power × hours; carbon = energy × emission factor.
Extending a laptop's service life from 3 to 5 years cuts its annual footprint by a quarter in the example.
